title: Wave-Particle Duality of Light
seo_title: Wave-Particle Duality Worksheets: Photons, E = hf and the Photoelectric Effect (Physics)
standard_text: Evaluate the claims, evidence, and reasoning behind the idea that electromagnetic radiation can be described either by a wave model or a particle model, and that for some situations one model is more useful than the other.
meta_desc: Free high school physics worksheets on wave-particle duality (NGSS HS-PS4-3): wave and particle models of light, photon energy E = hf and the photoelectric effect. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Light is both a wave and a particle.
key_sub: Interference needs the wave model; the photoelectric effect needs photons.
body_html:
How to think about it

Light acts like a wave and like a stream of particles (photons).

  • Wave model explains interference, diffraction and polarization.
  • Particle model explains the photoelectric effect: one photon frees one electron only if E = hf is above the work function.
  • Higher frequency (shorter wavelength) → more energy per photon. Brighter light → more photons, not stronger ones.
Example

Photon energy at 5 × 1014 Hz?

6.63 × 10−34 × 5 × 1014

Answer: 3.32 × 10−19 J

Example

3.0 eV photons on a 2.3 eV metal. Max KE?

3.0 − 2.3

Answer: 0.7 eV

Common mistakes

  • Thinking brighter light always frees electrons.
  • Thinking red photons have more energy than blue.
  • Thinking light must be only a wave or only a particle.

faq.a: Light shows wave behavior (interference, diffraction) in some experiments and particle behavior (photons) in others, so both models are needed.

faq.q: How do you find the energy of a photon?
faq.a: E = hf, where h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, or E = hc ÷ λ using the wavelength.

faq.q: Why doesn't bright red light free electrons from some metals?
faq.a: Each red photon has too little energy. Brighter light has more photons, but each one is still too weak.
